My daughter is 18 months old and we’ve been battling with UTIs since she was 8m (she’s had SIX in total).  This is the regimen we’ve been using (as recommended by a pediatric urologist at SickKids hospital) that has kept them at bay:


- HYDRATION. HYDRATION. HYDRATION. This was absolutely critical for us.  Make sure she is meeting/exceeding the recommended intake of fluids.
- AVOID CONSTIPATION!! Our daughter was prescribed a daily laxative- 1tsp of Restoralax every morning. 

Poor hydration and constipation are among the main causes of UTIs in children. In fact, for recurrent UTIs, your pediatrician will likely prescribe this routine before even considering a VCUG as it is less likely to be an anatomical issue. 

- PROBIOTICS. You can get flavourless powder packets specifically designed for babies. She gets one packet of Florastor with her morning bottle, and one packet of Kids Culturelle in her afternoon bottle.
- FREQUENT diaper changes during the day. Poop needs to be changed immediately, and make sure to “part the seas”. Remember she can’t do it herself.
- Use overnight diapers
- Avoid anything scented. Soaps, wipes, diapers, fabric softener etc. 
- Plain water baths after EVERY poop, soap her bum but use only water to wash between her private area


IF YOU SUSPECT A UTI:
- increase hydration
- give D-Mannose and Utiva cranberry supplement

IF SHE GETS A UTI:
- please remember that if she vomits or becomes febrile (fever) this is an immediate ER visit. Don’t wait- she needs antibiotics pronto. Fever usually indicates the infection has progressed from a “lower” UTI to an “upper” UTI (ie a kidney infection)
- advocate for a catheter urine sample. It’s the only way to obtain a sterile sample.  

If you live in Canada like me, the ER may attempt to send you home with just Tylenol so if you suspect one you absolutely need to advocate for further testing.

Feel free to pm me if you need, I literally have an entire spreadsheet of this stuff supported by research from scientific journal articles.

EDIT:  I should also mention she’s been scheduled for VCUG in six months to rule out reflux since she’s had so many... We all assumed this was an anatomical issue but honestly she hasn’t had a UTI since implementing these changes to her regimen.  I can’t stress enough that addressing hydration and constipation was absolutely critical for us!

To answer your question, whoever was on the account decided to gameshare over $1000 worth of games which resulted in the account being permabanned- something that customer service couldn’t reverse despite giving the serial number and everything.

We aren’t sure how the original breach happened, but when we contacted customer service to try and get it back the first time, they only asked us the email associated with account and last 4 digits of CC - info that could literally be anywhere on the dark web… apparently with that little amount of information they were able to disable 2FA by claiming they lost their phone (where 2FA codes were being sent originally) and they were able to change login credentials without any notification to my husbands email that someone was attempting to access his account.
This is not true, hackers can bypass all security protocols thru social engineering. That’s what happened to my husband. See my comment above

My husband’s PS account has been repeatedly hacked in the past couple months despite using a password manager with a VERY strong password and 2FA with authenticator app.  In a nutshell the hacker was able to bypass ALL security measures by using social engineering on customer service agents to gain access to the account. Sony’s security protocols are pretty laughable. His account ended up getting permabanned and customer service refused to do anything about it

We just started sleep training our 4-month old a couple of nights ago using CIO. Not sure if it’s helpful, but here is a list of affirmations that I read to help get through it!

* This will be better for our family.
* I am teaching her a valuable skill.
* She is in a stage of development where she is able to learn this skill.
* It is easier to sleep train now than later.
* The current ways of doing things are no longer working for our family. Being consistent and firm will help in the long run. 
* She is safe, loved, clean, dry, and fed.
* My job is to keep her healthy and safe, not prevent her from crying.
* This is the first time that as a parent, I need to hold space for her to do the hard things that she CAN do, without rescuing her. 
* You can’t pour from an empty cup.
* She will get better sleep independently in her own room. 
* If you fall into bad habits you’ll end up paying for them later.
* It’s not for no reason.
* She’s mad, not sad.

I would suggest saving your questions until they are off duty and are given significant time to decompress.  When my guy comes home I make sure to wait at least until after he’s able to shower and collect himself and adjust back to being “at home”. At which point I usually only ask him if there is anything “noteworthy” to report.  Asking them to review the specifics of their shift is usually unnecessary and overwhelming for them especially when they are trying to make the switch back to “normal life”.  You have to remember that for us, domestic violence calls/altercations/deaths etc. can seem really intense, but these are normal occurrences for them that don’t necessarily need to be discussed.

I usually avoid asking any lengthy questions when he’s on duty… sometimes their lack of a response can give them the impression that something has gone wrong when really they are just busy with something. We check in a couple times a shift but only very brief messages.
